Within about 60 days after this point, bearish doubts continued to exist around whether the company's replacement of auditors and supplementary financial reports were truly compliant.

Before and after Company A was expelled from the exchange's A100 index (late July 2024), was public opinion one-sided and alienated, and had become numb to repeated thunderstorms? Focusing on the technical game of 'can the 35-day moving average be held', stylized self-comforting rhetoric such as 'set a stop loss' and 'diversify risks' emerged?

In the 14 days before and after Company A was officially announced to be removed from the exchange's A100 index, did public opinion respond indifferently, focusing on the shrinking of passive position exposures, believing that when a stock 'disappears' from Fund B, 'pay attention to it and die', and there is no obvious support or opposition camp, and the silence of 'likes are attitudes' is a portrait?

Within 30 days after short-selling institution B announced its dissolution, did public opinion re-examine its grievances with company A? Some investors lamented that "the instigator has closed down" and ridiculed that the institution that was once called "media B" has retired. The overall mood has eased compared to before, and the long and short sides have tended to diverge?

In the 14 days after executive A first announced the 40 billion currency A revenue forecast for fiscal year 2026, and also lowered the guidance for fiscal year 2025, public opinion was full of jokes about "40 billion yuan pie, will you eat it?", the bearish group emphasized that "auditing agency B will never invest until the results are released", and the bullish group exaggerated the liquid cooling and chip manufacturer A's product A order imagination?

In the seven days after Company A submitted its annual report on October 1st to avoid delisting, did public opinion diverge in a 'survivor bias' style, labeling the reversal of its predicament as a 'textbook-level operation', and spread memes such as 'Organization B: I shorted you to the limit', mixed with insinuations against leveraged gamblers?

In the 30 days after Company A submitted its supplementary financial report in early October, did public opinion generally question the executives' suspicion of insider trading, pointing out that Persons B and C accurately cashed out nearly 6 million currency A when the annual report was delayed and the stock price changed, leading to the angry argument that "they ran away as soon as the delisting crisis was lifted"?

In the 30 days after co-founder F was arrested on smuggling charges in October 2025 and the board of directors launched an internal investigation, has public opinion turned to black humor on the topic of 'smuggling' (such as 'it's not smuggling, it's borrowing, and you have to pay back what you borrow'), and there has been a split in value between worshiping smugglers as 'national heroes' who meet the country's urgent need for X computing power and denouncing 'insiders'?

Within 30 days after Company A disclosed major flaws in its internal control over financial reporting in April 2025, did public opinion generally believe that this was just an inconsequential technical flaw, with full confidence in corporate governance, and sentiments that were mainly optimistic and bullish, with little doubt?

Within 30 days after Company A announced its fourth quarter financial report in March 2025, did the mainstream of public opinion turn bullish? Management was generally praised for its clever inventory strategy of "betting on old chips of chip vendor A" and believed that the price war had been effectively resolved?

Before and after Company A was removed from the exchange's A100 index, was public opinion in high spirits, with a large number of enthusiastic and bullish bargain-hunting voices, active interaction in the comment area, and unanimous optimism about its rebound?

Within 30 days after short-selling institution B announced its dissolution, did public opinion unanimously conclude that company A’s financial doubts have been completely overturned, the short-selling pressure has been permanently lifted, and the collective has turned firmly bullish?

time.desc: The exchange approved the listed company's application for an extension to submit financial documents, extending the cutoff by several months to temporarily avoid the risk of delisting.
Listed companies were officially removed from major market indexes because their market capitalization fell below inclusion criteria
Listed company submitted delayed annual report to regulators before cutoff, successfully avoiding forced delisting
Listed companies disclose that internal controls over financial reporting have major flaws and fail to operate effectively
Co-founder and CEO of public company arrested, faces multiple federal criminal charges
Listed company board member resigns, company appoints acting chief compliance officer
The independent director of a listed company launched an independent investigation to verify employees' suspected violations of export control regulations.

The board of directors of the listed company announced the appointment of a lead independent director to lead the internal investigation and hired external law firms and consulting agencies as independent consultants
The founder of the short-selling agency announced the dissolution of his long-established short-selling agency, saying that the phased tasks have been completed.
The company updated its plan to maintain its listing status and confirmed that it will submit its delayed annual report before the regulatory cutoff.
The company's management set a huge forward revenue target for the first time, and also lowered its revenue guidance for this fiscal year.
The company disclosed its fiscal year results, with net profit and revenue increasing significantly but gross profit margin declining.
The market questioned that many of the company's senior executives accurately reduced their holdings to cash out during the delay in annual reports and stock price changes.
Affected by the news of being removed from the major market index, Company A's stock price fell by about 8% that day.
Accounting Firm A, the original auditor of Company A, resigned from the audit job and expressed concerns about the internal control and governance of its financial reporting.
After Company A submitted its overdue financial report and lifted the risk of delisting, its stock price soared by more than 24% in after-hours trading.
Company A disclosed that its gross profit margin for the fiscal year fell from approximately 18% to approximately 13.8%, putting the quality of earnings under pressure.

After Company A completed the submission of all overdue documents, its stock price soared by more than 23% after the market closed. It plummeted by nearly 12% during the session as the delisting cutoff approached.
